title: Part of a collection, without copying it

prereqs.why: Every function here takes &[i64] rather than &Vec<i64>, and the halves and windows are slices of the same buffer.
A slice is a borrow, so everything about shared and exclusive access still applies to it.
You have built the growable array by hand, so you know what buffer a slice is pointing into.

statement:
Read `n` and `k`, then `n` integers. Write these two functions and use them:

```rust
fn sum(xs: &[i64]) -> i64
fn best_window(xs: &[i64], k: usize) -> Option<(usize, i64)>
```

`sum` takes a **slice**, not a `&Vec`, so the same function works on the whole
thing and on any part of it. `best_window` returns the starting index and sum of
the best run of `k` consecutive elements, or `None` if `k` is 0 or larger than
the data.

Print:

```
whole <sum of everything>
halves <sum of the first half> <sum of the second half>
left <the first half>
right <the second half>
window <start index> <sum>        or  window none
```

Split at `n / 2` using integer division, so an odd length puts the extra element
in the **right** half. On a tie for the best window, report the **earliest**
starting index.

```
input:   5 2            output:  whole 15
         1 2 3 4 5               halves 3 12
                                 left 1 2
                                 right 3 4 5
                                 window 3 9
```

Five elements split 2 and 3; the best pair is `4 5` starting at index 3.

### What a slice is

```
v: Vec<i64>        [ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ][ 4 ][ 5 ]      owns the heap buffer
                     ^
&v[1..4]           ptr --------+  len 3           borrows part of it
```

A `&[i64]` is two machine words: a pointer and a length. Making one copies
nothing, and the borrow checker guarantees the slice cannot outlive the buffer
it points into - so there is no way to hold a slice of a vector that has been
dropped or reallocated.

That is why **`&[T]` is the right parameter type** for a function that reads a
sequence. `&Vec<i64>` says "specifically a heap-allocated growable vector";
`&[i64]` says "any contiguous run of i64", which also accepts arrays, other
slices, and part of anything. A `&Vec<T>` converts to `&[T]` automatically, so
taking the slice costs the caller nothing.

### Boundary cases

`k = 0` and `k > n`, both of which give `window none`. `k = n`, where there is
exactly one window. `n = 0`, where both halves are empty, `sum` of an empty
slice is 0, and the `left`/`right` lines have nothing after the label. `n = 1`,
where the left half is empty. All-negative values, so the best window is the
least bad one and starting at 0 is not automatically right. A tie, which must
resolve to the earliest index.

### Platform assumptions

`n` is between 0 and 2000, `k` between 0 and 2000, and each value satisfies
`|value| <= 10^9`, so every sum fits in an `i64` with room to spare. `usize` is
64-bit on the platforms these problems run on, and the index arithmetic in a
sliding window is written so that nothing is subtracted below zero - which
matters because `usize` is unsigned and Rust panics on underflow in debug
builds.
hints: `v.split_at(mid)` returns a tuple of two slices in one call, and it panics if `mid > len` - which cannot happen for `len / 2`. You could also write `&v[..mid]` and `&v[mid..]`, which is the same thing.
For the window, compute the first sum directly with `sum(&xs[0..k])`, then slide: each step subtracts the element leaving the window and adds the one entering. That makes it O(n) instead of O(n*k).
Guard `k == 0 || k > xs.len()` first and return `None`. Without that guard, `xs.len() - k` underflows `usize` to an enormous number - which panics in a debug build and loops forever in a release one.

cases.expect:
whole 6
halves 1 5
left 1
right 2 3
window none
